intelDeltas.name: Fake Google Compensation / Settlement Payout Email
intelDeltas.summary: Email claims the recipient may qualify for a Google-related compensation payout due to regulatory or administrative settlement activity. Message uses official-looking reference codes and asks the recipient to provide personal information, with unrelated sender and reply domains.
intelDeltas.primaryLure: Free compensation payout or settlement award
absoluteIndicators: claimed Google sender with non-Google Return-Path or Envelope-From
claimed Google payout with unrelated reply-to or contact mailbox
compensation payout offered to generic user
request for personal or payment-related information to process payout
strongPhrases: required to provide the following information
weakPhrases: This message is available in English and Afrikaans
For other languages, please use Google Translate
headerSignals: Return-Path domain does not match claimed brand
Envelope-From domain does not match claimed brand
sending server domain does not match claimed brand
reply/contact mailbox uses unrelated domain
intelDeltas.userExplanation: This message claims to be from Google and offers a compensation payout, but the sender path and reply address are unrelated to Google. It asks for information to process money you did not apply for. Treat this as a scam. Do not reply, do not provide details, and do not click or submit anything.
intelDeltas.recommendedAction: Do not reply. Mark as spam/phishing. Delete the message. If details were already sent, contact the bank immediately and monitor accounts.

intelDeltas.name: AARTO Clone Payment Portal / Fine Threat Scam
intelDeltas.summary: Messages impersonate AARTO or RTIA, threaten licence-card or vehicle-disc restrictions, and push the recipient to a cloned payment portal. Current variants use urgent payment language, fake 50% discounts or penalty waivers, and may ask for R250 or other immediate payments.
intelDeltas.primaryLure: Avoid licence or vehicle-disc restrictions by paying an urgent traffic fine
absoluteIndicators: AARTO payment demand sends the user to a non-official website instead of online.aarto.gov.za
message is presented as NATS Online Vehicle License Disc Renewal
claimed AARTO payment portal is a cloned or unrelated domain
strongPhrases: Final Notice: Action Required to Avoid Additional Penalties
vehicle licence disc will be blocked
NATS Online Vehicle License Disc Renewal
headerSignals: AARTO or RTIA claim with a payment link outside online.aarto.gov.za
AARTO-branded link using .com, .co.za or .online instead of the official AARTO portal
intelDeltas.userExplanation: This message uses AARTO or RTIA branding to create payment pressure. Current scam variants threaten licence or vehicle-disc restrictions and send people to cloned payment pages. Do not use the link in the message. Check the infringement directly through the official AARTO or RTIA channels.
intelDeltas.recommendedAction: Do not click or pay through the message. Verify the infringement independently at the official AARTO portal or through RTIA. If card or banking details were entered, contact the bank immediately.

intelDeltas.name: SARS Tax Return / Assessment / Summons Phishing Wave
intelDeltas.summary: 2026 filing-season scams use Tax Return Notification, Notice of Assessment or ITA34 wording, refund claims, settlement demands and High Court summons language. The scam pushes recipients toward links, payment requests, banking-detail capture or HTML attachments that imitate SARS correspondence.
intelDeltas.primaryLure: Tax refund, assessment action or urgent SARS compliance
absoluteIndicators: SARS-branded message requests banking credentials, PIN, OTP or eFiling password
SARS-branded message uses an .htm or .html attachment to collect details
SARS refund or assessment message redirects to a non-SARS website for claim or verification
headerSignals: sender domain is not sars.gov.za
reply-to domain differs from the claimed SARS sender
SARS-branded message contains an external non-SARS claim or payment link
intelDeltas.userExplanation: This message uses current SARS filing-season wording but asks you to act through a link, attachment or payment path that should not be trusted from the message itself. Open SARS eFiling or the SARS MobiApp independently and verify the notice there.
intelDeltas.recommendedAction: Do not click the message link or open HTML attachments. Verify the notice directly through SARS eFiling, the SARS MobiApp or a verified SARS contact channel.

intelDeltas.name: FSCA / Licensed FSP Impersonation Investment Scam
intelDeltas.summary: Fraudsters impersonate licensed financial services providers, reuse legitimate FSP numbers and staff identities, and move victims into WhatsApp or Telegram groups for fake share, forex, crypto or trading offers. Some variants use deepfake or AI-generated media and official-looking regulatory references.
intelDeltas.primaryLure: Exclusive or regulator-backed investment opportunity with unusually high returns
absoluteIndicators: claimed FSCA or licensed FSP investment offer requires payment through an unsolicited WhatsApp or Telegram group
FSP number is used as proof of legitimacy while payment is directed outside the verified provider
regulator-branded recovery process requires funding a cryptocurrency wallet
headerSignals: claimed FSP sender uses an unrelated domain
investment conversation is moved to WhatsApp or Telegram
regulator identity is used to justify a payment or crypto-wallet step
intelDeltas.userExplanation: The message borrows the identity of a legitimate financial provider or regulator to make an unsolicited investment look authorised. A real FSP number or familiar company name does not prove that the person contacting you is authorised.
intelDeltas.recommendedAction: Do not deposit or install an app from the message. Verify the provider and representative independently through the FSCA and the provider's own published contact details.

intelDeltas.name: Bank Fraud-Team Safe / Vault Account Impersonation
intelDeltas.summary: Fraudsters impersonate bank fraud staff, often with spoofed caller ID or convincing AI-assisted communication, and claim suspicious activity requires the victim to move money to a safe or vault account, approve a transaction, scan a QR code or reveal an OTP.
intelDeltas.primaryLure: Protect funds from an alleged active compromise
absoluteIndicators: bank fraud team instructs recipient to move money to a safe or vault account
bank fraud team asks recipient to scan a QR code to secure the banking profile
bank representative asks for OTP, PIN or transaction approval for a transaction the recipient did not initiate
headerSignals: caller ID alone is presented as proof that the bank is calling
bank-branded message redirects security action to WhatsApp, QR code or an external link
intelDeltas.userExplanation: A bank does not need you to transfer your money to another account to keep it safe. Fraudsters use urgent fraud-alert stories, spoofed caller IDs and increasingly convincing messages to make that instruction feel legitimate.
intelDeltas.recommendedAction: End the call or conversation. Do not transfer money, scan a QR code or share an OTP. Contact the bank using the number in the banking app, on the back of the card or on the bank's verified website.

intelDeltas.name: Fake Proof of Payment / Overpayment / Voucher Extraction
intelDeltas.summary: A buyer places an urgent order, supplies a fake or altered proof of payment, pressures the business to release or deliver goods before funds clear, and may deliberately overpay so the difference can be extracted as a refund, voucher, prepaid value or payment to a third party. The scam succeeds when staff treat a payment document as proof that cleared funds exist.
intelDeltas.primaryLure: Urgent paid order that appears safe because a bank-branded proof of payment is supplied
likelyFollowUp: request to release goods before payment reflects
claim that payment will reflect shortly
FLASH voucher or prepaid voucher request
request to send voucher PIN or code
request to pay the excess to a third party
absoluteIndicators: proof of payment plus instruction to release or deliver goods before funds reflect
claimed overpayment plus request to return the difference as a voucher, prepaid value or third-party payment
bank-branded payment confirmation contains a false bank contact number and is used to pressure release of goods
headerSignals: payment amount does not match the underlying invoice or order
payment date is inconsistent with the order or invoice date
beneficiary name on the payment confirmation does not match the intended business
bank contact details on the payment confirmation do not match the bank's verified contact details
currency formatting or document text contains unusual inconsistencies
funds do not reflect in the recipient's actual bank account
intelDeltas.userExplanation: A proof of payment is only a document; it is not cleared money. This scam uses a convincing payment confirmation and urgency to get goods, cash or prepaid value released before the bank account actually receives the funds. If the buyer also claims to have overpaid and asks for the difference as a voucher or refund, the risk is critical.
intelDeltas.recommendedAction: Do not release goods, deliver, refund, buy vouchers or send prepaid codes until the payment is visible as cleared funds in the business bank account. Verify suspicious payment confirmations independently with the bank using verified contact details.
